sources.news_title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race
sources.text:
Democrat Scott Colom has won election to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi, according to a race call by the Associated Press, narrowly defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
After more than a week of counting outstanding, absentee ballots and affidavit — or provisional — ballots, Colom won the closest Senate race in the country by just a few thousand votes.
Loading...
In a midterm full of stunning upsets for Democrats, Colom's victory underscores a dramatic shift in the political landscape across the South driven by a surge of Black voter turnout.
Mississippi has the highest share of Black voters in the country, at close to 40%, but President Trump won the state by 23 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in more than 40 years and hasn't sent a Black senator to Washington since Reconstruction.
The state's rural, agriculture-heavy economy was disproportionately impacted by rising prices, and saw millions in investment from both parties, particularly in the final weeks of the race. Colom, a district attorney, made cost of living a centerpiece of his campaign message, decrying "Cindy High-Prices" as bad for Mississippi.
Unlike most other contested Senate races that flipped, Mississippi did not see much national money or attention until the closing days of the election. That included a rally in the final week by President Trump and high-profile visits from former Vice President Kamala Harris, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and other Democrats. The Cook Political Report had the race rated as Likely Republican going into election night.
Colom told NPR earlier this month that a lack of investment from national Democrats until the last minute was a mistake.
"The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause, we've been a betrayed cause," he said. "The Democratic Party has not been trying to win Mississippi. Let's stop kidding ourselves, right? They spent hundreds of millions of dollars in other states. They spent almost nothing in Mississippi."
Colom's campaign was a contrast in style from Hyde-Smith, who rarely spoke to reporters in Washington and had minimal presence in the state.
When asked about high beef prices earlier this year, Hyde-Smith — a cattle rancher and onetime state agriculture commissioner — said that "you have so many other proteins to choose from."
That led to a viral campaign ad from Colom, which featured several people expressing disbelief at the senator's suggestion to "pick another protein." Instead, the ad said, it was time to "pick another senator."

sources.news_title: Mississippi Picks Another Senator Making Scott Colom the First Black Person to Hold the Seat Since Reconstruction
sources.text:
After over a week of making sure every legal vote counted, Democrat Scott Colom can now say he is a Mississippi U.S. Senator.
The district attorney for Mississippi’s 16th Judicial District beat Incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) by nearly 4,700 votes, according to The Associated Press.
Colom will be the first Black U.S. senator for Mississippi since Blanche Bruce, who served in the Senate from 1875 to 1881, during and post-Reconstruction era. He will also be the first Democrat in the seat since 1989, following in the footsteps of John Stennis.
The nail-bitting race came down to counties having to verify affidavit ballots, which are provisional votes coming from people whose eligibility election workers could not immediately verify at the polls. It’s often because a voter lacks an acceptable photo ID or did not appear on the voter rolls.
Mississippi election officials also had five business days to receive and count absentee mail-in ballots, provided voters postmarked them by Election Day.
Colom always felt very confident that he’d be heading to Washington as the state’s next senator.
“Where we are, where the ballots are, we’re gonna win,” Colom said while addressing his supporters the day after the election. “This is our election. We’ve won it. The people have done it. They’ve decided to go in a new direction. I’m confident of that.”
Meanwhile, Hyde-Smith had been quiet about the elections until reporters caught up with her at the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday.
“We are still counting votes and there’s a few thousand out, and we feel confident,” she said.
Colom took a different view, suggesting Hyde-Smith was refusing to reckon with the possibility of losing her seat.
“At some point we have to put the people of Mississippi above our personal feelings and partisan politics,” he said.
Final results show that Colom was able to secure his seat by flipping at least 18 counties that previously voted for Donald Trump. This includes Forrest County which was named after the Ku Klux Klan’s first Grand Wizard, Nathan Bedford Forrest.
Many credit Colom’s victory to his outside-of-the-box ads and young voter turnout. His campaign focused on economic policies, and he presented himself as a moderate, which helped him gain support in historically Republican areas.
Despite the close race, there will be no automatic runoff. Mississippi’s election handbook and state law does not outline a process for contesting the results of a general election for the U.S. Senate.
However, according to Secretary of State Michael Watson, candidates can examine ballot materials after certification to look for irregularities.
It seems as though Hyde-Smith will not go that route. In a video statement on X, she conceded.
“While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Colom, and wish him well, as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

sources.news_title: Democrat Colom will be Mississippi's first Black senator in more than 100 years, AP projects
sources.text:
Colom's win will be the eighth Senate pickup for Democrats.
Democrat Scott Colom will upset Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, The Associated Press projected Wednesday, flipping a Republican seat in a ruby-red state.
With 99% of the expected vote reported, Colom leads with 49.2%, and Hyde-Smith has 48.7% of the vote, with Colom leading by about 4,700 votes.
Colom's win is the eighth Democratic pickup in the Senate with the race in Alaska yet to be decided.
Hyde-Smith has called Colom to concede, a campaign spokesperson confirmed to ABC News.
In a video posted on her campaign account Wednesday evening, Hyde-Smith said, “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
Colom is a district attorney for four counties along the Mississippi-Alabama state line and a former nominee to become a U.S. district judge. He will be Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.
While his campaign had initially been seen as a long shot, Colom built up more buzz in the last few months of the campaign, appearing with major party figures such as former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris. He also went viral with a campaign video where he mocked Hyde-Smith over comments she made about choosing other options for proteins because of high beef prices.
Hyde-Smith, who was running for a second full term, campaigned with President Donald Trump during a rally in October and insisted she was the right choice for the state.
Colom and Hyde-Smith had some history even before Colom's Senate run, as she blocked his nomination for federal judge in 2023, although Colom has said he has forgiven her for doing so.
Colom told ABC News in an interview after Election Day that his campaign didn't get much attention or resources outside Mississippi until about a month ago because some in his party couldn't fathom that Democrats could flip a Senate seat in the Magnolia State.
He says that forced him to build a ground game which took him to many areas of the state and put him face-to-face with a lot of voters. He said many of those voters gravitated towards him because they were tired of broken promises in Washington.
"The voters were betrayed. That gave us an opportunity to compete everywhere. And for me, I wasn't afraid to call that out, and I wasn't also afraid to say what I was going to do," he said.
Both campaigns and their associated political parties had indicated after Election Day, as the margin between them remained tight, that they were ready for potential litigation in the race, particularly over provisional ballots that both sides estimated could number in the thousands.

sources.news_title: Democrat Colom defeats incumbent Republican in Mississippi Senate race
sources.text:
Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Mr. Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any U.S. state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South.
The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Mr. Colom’s favour after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Ms. Hyde-Smith, 67, said in a two-minute concession speech posted online. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
A spokesman for the senator said she called Mr. Colom to congratulate him and concede before the video was shared publicly.
Mr. Colom scheduled a victory celebration with supporters Wednesday night in Jackson.
Democrats reclaim Latino voters in Texas, other pivotal midterm races
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Mr. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state’s large Black population, discontent with the economy and Ms. Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.
“They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Mr. Colom said in the campaign’s closing stretch.
Mr. Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.
“It’s got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America – a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better,” he said.
Party leaders hailed the senator-elect’s triumph, with nods to the South’s emerging battleground status after other upset victories from North Carolina to Texas.
“Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done,” Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online. “Along with his staff and volunteers, Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and reimagined what’s possible for Democrats in the South.”
Former president Bill Clinton, a native Arkansan who campaigned with Mr. Colom days before the election, addressed the senator-elect on social media, saying he won “because you believe in the promise of your state’s people. And they believed in you right back.”
Vera Finley was among those supporters, and she arrived early Wednesday to Colom’s victory party.
“I am here to celebrate my parents and my grandparents. I am not one generation out of the cotton fields,” Ms. Finley said. “Both of my parents picked cotton. And my great grandmother was sold here as a slave from Virginia to here. So I am so excited to be on this side of history.”
Another Mississippian, NAACP President Derrick Johnson, issued a statement saying the state’s voters “made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out.”
“In a state that has witnessed some of the nation’s most difficult battles for voting rights, Black voters once again demonstrated the power of civic engagement and the strength of our democracy,” Mr. Johnson said.
Despite Mr. Schumer’s support, the contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, drawing attention and money months after Black senators, including Georgia’s Raphael Warnock and Maryland’s Angela Alsobrooks, first urged donors and party leaders to see the contest as winnable.
The son of a onetime Republican who worked for president Ronald Reagan, Mr. Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Ms. Hyde-Smith’s vulnerabilities crystallized.
He produced one of the year’s most widely circulated ads. After Ms. Hyde-Smith seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Mr. Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they’d “pick another senator instead.”
When Mr. Trump came to Corinth, Miss., in late October for a rally with Ms. Hyde-Smith, Mr. Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.
Later that evening, when Mr. Trump called Ms. Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: “Is this not the best President in our lifetime?”
Then she stepped away.
Mr. Colom’s appearance outside the rally tracked his strategy of criticizing Mr. Trump’s policies – especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers – without taking personal jabs at the President or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Ms. Hyde-Smith, framing her as a nonentity in Washington – a critique that resonated in a state that has been accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.
There is some irony to Ms. Hyde-Smith losing to Mr. Colom. In 2022, then-president Joe Biden nominated Mr. Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi’s senior Republican Senator Roger Wicker and former Governor Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.
Ms. Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Mr. Colom’s confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president’s choices for federal judicial positions in their home state. Mr. Colom said his campaign was never about getting even with Ms. Hyde-Smith.
Democrat James Talarico’s victory in Texas sends a shock wave through the GOP
The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family.
“In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection,” Mr. Colom said, telling the story of Mr. Evers’ military service at Normandy in the Second World War, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction.
“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Mr. Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honour everyone who died for that right.”
Mr. Schumer helped Mr. Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate.
Former president Bill Clinton and former vice-president Kamala Harris campaigned on Mr. Colom’s behalf in the campaign’s closing weeks.
Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi’s general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbours. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win re-election by a margin of just 3 percentage points.
Mr. Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats’ usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.
Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Mr. Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.
Then-governor Phil Bryant first appointed Ms. Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Mr. Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who’d also been Mississippi’s first Black congressman since Reconstruction.
During the extended vote count, Mr. Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Mr. Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story.
“My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young Black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I’ve done that they shouldn’t get a chance.”

Democrat Scott Colom seals historic win in Mississippi Senate race
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.
Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be elected to the US Senate in more than 140 years.
Only a few thousand votes separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Across the room, filled with people embracing, Amber Thomas sat, revelling in the victory.
"When you fight, you win," Thomas said. "Right now, I am overwhelmed with joy."
The result wipes away a Republican winning streak in the Magnolia State that dates back to 1982.
The contest was never expected to be this close, with Hyde-Smith running for re-election in a state that President Donald Trump won in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.
But Democrats have scored a series of major wins in these midterm elections, taking control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

Polls suggest this was due in large part to voter frustrations with the economy and the Iran war under President Trump.

The Democrat campaigned aggressively, visiting all of Mississippi's 82 counties.
Hyde-Smith's campaign assailed Colom as a puppet of billionaire liberal donor George Soros, whose family has helped fund the Democrat's political campaigns.
The Republican was criticised for a lack of public appearances.

History made as black Democrat wins Senate race in deep red Mississippi
Washington: Democrat Scott Colom will be the next US senator for Mississippi, flipping a traditionally deep-red state and becoming the first black man to hold that office since the aftermath of the Civil War more than 150 years ago.
After a count that took more than a week, the Associated Press declared Colom the winner at 6pm Wednesday (10am Thursday, AEDT).
He defeated incumbent Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, and delivered the Democrats an eighth new seat in the 100-seat Senate to increase the party’s total to 55.
Colom was considered an outside chance weeks ago, being several points behind Hyde-Smith in the polls, but became more of a dark horse as the campaign went on.
He was aided by simple but effective advertisements, including one that played on the rising cost of beef – a potent issue in what is considered America’s poorest state.
Asked about beef prices in a television interview in February, Hyde-Smith said: “You know, you have so many proteins to choose from.”
Colom’s campaign turned that into a viral ad featuring a man with a southern drawl cooking on the barbecue. “Pick another protein?” he asks. “Shiiii ... I’d rather pick another senator instead.”
The result in Mississippi not only caps a dramatic national blue wave with generational impact on US politics, but marks a historic moment for the Deep South state.
The last Democrat elected to the US Senate from Mississippi was John Stennis, who served from 1947 to 1989 and was elected for the final time in 1982.
Like other Democrats at the time, Stennis was an avowed racial segregationist for most of his career, though he supported an extension of the Voting Rights Act in the 1980s.
Mississippi sent two black men to the US Senate in the 1870s, during the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Both were Republicans and elected by the state legislature, not the public.
Civil rights activist Flonzie Brown-Wright, who in the 1960s became the first black woman elected to public office in Mississippi since the Reconstruction, told The Financial Times last week: “It just feels like our time has come.”
Colom’s victory adds to a haul of Democratic wins in the Deep South, including Annie Andrews, who defeated Darline Graham for the Senate seat in South Carolina, and Keisha Lance Bottoms, the new governor of Georgia, who also became the first black woman elected governor of a US state.
In Louisiana, another deep red southern state, the Democratic Senate candidate came within two percentage points of victory. Democrats also had rare wins in Texas, Kansas and Iowa, among other states.
Hyde-Smith was initially elected to the Mississippi state senate as a conservative Democrat, before switching parties. In 2018, she filled a vacancy in the US Senate and was re-elected in 2020.
Last week, on election night, Hyde-Smith appeared to pre-emptively declare victory, despite also saying that it remained too close to call.
“I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being a US senator,” she told her election night function.
But in a video message after the final result, Hyde-Smith said she respected Mississippi voters’ decision and congratulated Colom.
“While my time in the United States Senate may be coming to an end, my love for Mississippi and my determination to stand up for what is right never will,” she said.

sources.text:
Mississippi elects its first Black senator in 150 years giving Democrats a 55-seat majority
Democrat Scott Colom defeats Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in nail-biter Senate race
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Join today
Already a member? Log in
Blanche Bruce was born into slavery in 1841. He later served one term as a U.S. senator from Mississippi. He was the second — and the last — Black senator from a state at the violent heart of the nation’s civil rights struggle.
Nearly 150 years later, Mississippi voters elected Scott Colom, who is poised to be the first Black candidate elected to the U.S. Senate from the Deep South state since the aftermath of the Civil War.
Colom’s election will oust Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and add to an explosive series of Democratic victories in midterm elections that have shifted the balance of power in Congress and are likely to derail the final two years of Donald Trump’s administration.
Colom’s victory also is a seismic rebuke against threats to the ballot box and the relics of a bloody history that made Mississippi among the hardest places to vote in the country.
Mississippi was one of two states alongside Alaska where Americans are still eagerly anticipating the results of Senate elections more than one week after Election Day. Democrats are projected to hold at least 55 seats in the Senate and more than 255 seats in the House of Representatives.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said in a video statement Wednesday night. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
This week, all eyes were on Hinds County, Mississippi’s most populous county and a Democratic stronghold that spans the state’s capital of Jackson, where election officials tallied remaining ballots.
Most of the remaining ballots in the state are affidavit ballots, which voters cast if they did not bring identification with them to the polls or were listed as having an inactive voter registration.
Voters cast 2,426 affidavit ballots in Hinds County. Election officials rejected 1,609 of them, and the vast majority of accepted ballots were cast for Colom.
By Wednesday night, Colom’s lead in the state increased to more than 5,000 over Hyde-Smith, with 99 percent of ballots counted, according to unofficial results from the Associated Press. Colom’s campaign and election analysts determined outstanding ballots would not make up the difference.
Mississippi law does not provide for a recount process for Senate races.
The state — marked by a lethal history of voter suppression — is also one of only three states that do not allow early in-person voting and among a dozen that do not allow universal mail-in voting. Republicans have also tried to throw out mail-in ballots that were postmarked before Election Day but arrived later, a challenge that the Supreme Court rejected earlier this year.
Mississippi also has retained a Jim Crow-era law that imposes a lifetime ban from the ballot box against anyone convicted of certain felony crimes, a law that currently disenfranchises nearly 70,000 disproportionately-Black residents — or about 3 percent of the state’s eligible voting population.
Roughly 40 percent of Mississippi residents are Black, but the state’s political makeup for decades has largely been made up of white officials at the state and federal level.
According to the Movement Advancement Project’s ranking of voter access by state, Mississippi is dead last.
“Scott Colom’s historic win is the product of years of organizing and community engagement by groups on the ground, who laid the foundation for the change we’re seeing today,” said Amir Badat with voting rights advocacty group Fair Fight.
“Black voters in Mississippi overcame incredible obstacles — long lines, broken voting machines, voting location changes, and more than 230,000 voters recklessly made inactive and essentially forced into a second class ballot — and still turned out in historic numbers,” Baday said. They made it clear that their voices must be heard, and they took action to win the change they deserve.”
In 1870, the Mississippi legislature sent Hiram Revels to fill one of the state’s two Senate seats left vacant after the Civil War. The country’s first Black senator filled the seat previously held by Confederate Albert Brown, a slaveholder who championed what he called the “blessings of slavery” beyond American borders.
Several years later, Blanche Bruce was elected to the seat once held by Confederate President Jefferson Davis.
But in the turbulent aftermath of the Civil War and emancipation, from white militia terror during Reconstruction through the decades-long Civil Rights movement, Mississippi never elected a Black senator again.
The state’s last Democratic senator was aligned with the conservative Dixiecrats before a massive political realignment flipped the party platforms in the wake of civil rights progress and New Deal economic policies.
John C. Stennis — the state’s last Democratic senator — opposed school integration, voted against the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act, and tried to block the creation of Martin Luther King Jr. Day as a federal holiday. He served for 41 years until his retirement in 1988.
In 1934, as a trial prosecutor before his political career, Stennis was at the center of a murder case that led to a landmark Supreme Court ruling that determined confessions could not be coerced through violence and torture.
Stennis had argued for a jury to convict three Black men accused of murdering a white man. One of the men on trial was non-fatally hanged twice and beaten while in custody. The others were also beaten until they confessed.
They were each found guilty and sentenced to death before their convictions were overturned.
Like Stennis, Colom worked as a prosecutor and a judge before launching his political career.
Colom, a seventh-generation Mississippian, was nominated by then-President Joe Biden to serve as a federal judge for the Northern District of Mississippi in 2022.
But his nomination was blocked by one of the state’s two Republican senators: Cindy Hyde-Smith.
“To see him now elected to the very Senate where his nomination was blocked is especially meaningful and a testament to his perseverance and the trust Mississippians have placed in his leadership,” said Rep. Bennie Thompson, who has been the only Democrat in Mississippi's congressional delegation since 2011.
“Having another Mississippi Democrat alongside me in Congress who understands the needs of Mississippians means a great deal,” Thompson said. “Together, we will fight to improve access to health care, strengthen public education, expand economic opportunities, and ensure our rural and underserved communities are not left behind.”

Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state’s first Black US senator since Reconstruction
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it yielded immediate echoes around the country. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South.
The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom’s favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith, 67, said in a two-minute concession speech posted online. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
A spokesman for the senator said she called Colom to congratulate him and concede before the video was shared publicly.
Colom scheduled a victory celebration with supporters Wednesday night in Jackson.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state’s large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.
“They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign’s closing stretch.
Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.
“It’s got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better,” he said.
National Democrats and activists celebrate along with Colom
Party leaders hailed the senator-elect’s triumph, with nods to the South’s emerging battleground status after other upset victories from North Carolina to Texas.
“Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done,” Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online. “Along with his staff and volunteers, Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what’s possible for Democrats in the South.”
Former President Bill Clinton, a native Arkansan who campaigned with Colom days before the election, addressed the senator-elect on social media, saying he won “because you believe in the promise of your state’s people. And they believed in you right back.”
NAACP President Derrick Johnson, who lives in Mississippi, issued a statement saying: “Mississippi voters made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out. ... In a state that has witnessed some of the nation’s most difficult battles for voting rights, Black voters once again demonstrated the power of civic engagement and the strength of our democracy.”
A race Washington once viewed as a long shot
Despite Schumer’s support, the contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, drawing attention and money months after Black senators, including Georgia’s Raphael Warnock and Maryland’s Angela Alsobrooks, first urged donors and party leaders to see the contest as winnable.
The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith’s vulnerabilities crystallized.
He produced of the year’s most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they’d “pick another senator instead.”
When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.
Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: “Is this not the best president in our lifetime?”
Then she stepped away.
Colom’s appearance outside the rally tracked his strategy of criticizing Trump’s policies — especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a nonentity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state that has been accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.
There is some irony to Hyde-Smith losing to Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi’s senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.
Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom’s confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president’s choices for federal judicial positions in their home state. Colom said his campaign was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.
Colom called on Mississippi’s history
The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family.
“In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection,” Colom said, telling the story of Evers’ military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction.
“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”
Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate.
Former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned on Colom’s behalf in the campaign’s closing weeks.
Despite Republicans’ domination, the path was always there
With the largest share of Black voters of any state, Mississippi’s general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbors. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.
Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats’ usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.
Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.
Then-Gov. Phil Bryant first appointed Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who’d also been Mississippi’s first Black congressman since Reconstruction.
During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story.
“My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young Black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I’ve done that they shouldn’t get a chance.”
